_comment: All LLM prompt text for the assistant app, externalized from prompts.py so wording can be tuned without touching Python logic. Loaded once at import time by prompts.py, which fills in the {placeholder} slots below with dynamic content (profile text, job details, user notes, etc.) via str.format() — see prompts.py for the actual substitution logic. Keep every {placeholder} name here in sync with what prompts.py passes in; a rename on one side without the other raises a KeyError at generation time, not silently.
anti_fabrication_rule: CRITICAL RULE, follow this above all else: you must NEVER invent a specific employer, job title, project name, date, metric/statistic, or contact detail (name, email, phone) that is not explicitly written in the candidate profile below. If the profile does not mention a specific past job, project, or accomplishment, you have zero permission to describe one, even a vague or generic-sounding one — do not write "a previous project", "in my last role", "I've had experience with...", or anything implying unstated specific experience. The same applies to a specific skill or tool the job asks for: if the profile does not show it, you must NOT claim the candidate has it, even softly. Instead say so plainly and pivot to genuine willingness/ability to learn it — e.g. "I haven't worked directly with Terraform, but I pick up infrastructure tooling quickly and would be glad to build that skill on the job." Never invent a way around a gap; name it and turn it into an honest, forward-looking sentence. Speaking in honest general terms (interest in the role, understanding of what it involves, willingness to learn) is correct and expected wherever the profile doesn't back up something more specific — it is not a worse output, it is the required one.
skill_whitelist_template:
KNOWN, VERIFIED SKILLS/TECHNOLOGIES — this is the ONLY set you may say or imply the candidate has any expertise in: {skill_whitelist}
If something the job below asks for is not in this exact list, it is a gap, full stop — per the rule above, name it honestly and pivot to willingness to learn, no matter how strongly the job title or role name might seem to suggest otherwise. Concrete real example of the exact mistake to never repeat: applying to a job titled "SAP Entwickler" (SAP Developer) does NOT mean the candidate has SAP or ABAP experience — unless "SAP" or "ABAP" literally appears in the list above, the candidate has never worked with either, no matter how strongly the job title implies it, and you must not claim or even softly imply otherwise. Do not write anything like "as a seasoned ABAP/4 and ABAP OO developer" or "I have developed a strong foundation in ABAP/4 and ABAP OO programming languages" when ABAP is not in the list above — this exact fabrication happened once already, for this exact kind of job-title-implies-a-tech-stack mismatch, and must never happen again for any technology, not just this one.

cover_letter.body_template:
{anti_fabrication_rule}

{skill_whitelist_block}

Write the BODY of a cover letter for this candidate applying to this job — just the body paragraphs, not a
full letter (the name/contact header, date, salutation, and signature are added separately by code afterward,
not by you — do not write any of those, see the exact instructions on this below). This requirement-matching
is the single most important part of the task: read the job description below closely, identify the concrete
requirements, responsibilities, and skills it actually asks for, and address the most important 3-5 of them
directly and specifically — naming the real requirement and connecting it to a real, matching piece of the
candidate's profile (a skill, a certification, a language, a project, a specific piece of experience from any
job listed — whatever is genuinely there, read the profile's FULL detail below, not just a high-level skim of
it, since the specific match is often in a job's description rather than the skills list). A letter that only
restates the candidate's own background without engaging with what THIS job is asking for is a failure —
matching the two is the entire point, not a nice-to-have. For any important requirement the profile does not
support, follow the anti-fabrication rule above: name the gap honestly and pivot to genuine willingness/ability
to learn it, rather than skipping it or vaguely implying the candidate already has it. The candidate's listed
interests can also strengthen a genuine connection to the role/company where they actually fit — don't force
it if they don't.

Write it in the candidate's own voice, first person, as if they wrote it themselves — not as an AI assistant
describing them. Avoid generic AI-cover-letter clichés. This means banning whole SENTENCE SHAPES, not just
specific wordings — swapping in different words after the same template is still the same cliché, and doing
that to dodge a banned phrase while keeping its structure is exactly what NOT to do. Banned shapes, with one
example each of the substitution game to specifically not play:
- "I am writing to express my interest in ___" (or "I am reaching out regarding ___")
- "I am a highly motivated/dedicated/passionate ___ professional"
- "I believe I would be a great/strong/excellent fit/candidate for ___"
- "I'm [excited/thrilled/eager/intrigued] about the prospect of ___" — no matter what fills the blank
  ("working in...", "bringing my experience to...", "contributing to...", anything else), the shape itself is
  the cliché and stays banned regardless of the words used to fill it in
- Quoting the job posting's own generic corporate phrasing back at it (e.g. a posting says "complex technical
  environment" — do not reuse that phrase; describe the actual work in the candidate's own words instead)
- "[list of skills] make/makes me a strong/great/excellent candidate for this role" — a template with the
  nouns swapped out, not writing that engages with the job
If a sentence would still basically make sense with the job/company swapped for a different one, or with its
specific nouns replaced by placeholders, it's generic — rewrite it grounded in an actual detail from the job
description or the candidate's real background instead. Open specifically and naturally — do NOT start with a
salutation like "Dear ..." (that's added separately, see above) or a "Dear Hiring Manager" style opener; jump
straight into the first substantive sentence. Close simply — do NOT write "Sincerely," or any signature/closing
line, that's also added separately.

Do not just list skills and then assert they make the candidate qualified — that's the same generic pattern
under a different shape. For each requirement you're matching, make the connection causal and specific: not
"I have X, Y, Z, which make me a strong candidate," but why the specific thing the job needs is something this
specific piece of background actually addresses — e.g. instead of "My experience with Java and Spring Boot
make me a strong candidate for this role," write something like "Since the role centers on testing services
built on Spring Boot, the years I've spent writing integration tests against exactly that stack mean there's
no ramp-up time." Show the reasoning, don't just assert the conclusion.

Vary sentence structure — don't make every sentence the same length and shape. Around 250-400 words. Plain
text only, no markdown, no headers, no bullet points, no placeholder brackets like [Company Name] — use the
real details given below throughout.

CANDIDATE PROFILE:
{profile}

JOB:
{application}
{notes_block}
Respond with ONLY the cover letter body paragraphs and nothing else — no salutation, no signature, no
meta-commentary or preamble of any kind, in any form, anywhere in the response (not just at the very start).
This includes, and is not limited to: "Here is the cover letter body:", "Sure, here's...", and — confirmed
live as a real failure, not a hypothetical one — narrating your own approach instead of just taking it, e.g.
"Since the candidate profile is empty, I will write a letter that focuses on...", "I'll focus on genuine
interest since there isn't much background to draw on", or any sentence that mentions "the candidate profile"
as a concept. A real person writing their own cover letter never explains their own writing strategy inside
the letter — they just write it. Start directly with the first sentence of the letter itself, as if any
narration about how you're approaching this never occurred to you.
Reminder: {anti_fabrication_rule}

answer.empty_profile_note: The candidate profile below is EMPTY — no resume has been uploaded yet. Answer honestly in general terms instead (motivation, understanding of the role, transferable qualities). Do not describe any specific past job, project, or accomplishment under any circumstances. Just answer in general terms directly — never mention that the profile is empty, that background wasn't provided, or explain why the answer is general; a real person answering out loud would never say that out loud, they'd just answer.
